content: In phonetics, the term vocalic r refers to a rhotic segment, such as [ɚ] or [ɝ], that functions as the nucleus of a syllable. This phenomenon is observed in several languages, including Slavic languages like Croatian and Czech, as well as in English and Mandarin Chinese. In these languages, the vocalic r is characterized as an r-colored vowel, which is acoustically defined by a low third formant frequency. In rhotic varieties of English, such as General American English, vocalic r appears in words like butter and church. In the ancient Indian language Sanskrit, there were both short and long forms of a vowel sound referred to as vocalic r. These are represented in Devanagari script as ऋ (short form) and ॠ (long form), and in IAST transliteration as ṛ and ṝ. This sound is believed to correspond to the original vocalic l or r in Proto-Indo-European. Classical Sanskrit grammarians classified this vowel as retroflex, and its pronunciation is thought to have been a retroflex approximant [ɻ] around 500 BCE. Earlier grammarians, however, described its sound during the Vedic period as velar. When Sanskrit words containing this sound were borrowed into modern Indo-Aryan languages like Hindi or Nepali, the pronunciation shifted to [ri] (short form) or [r̩ː] (long form), resulting in forms like Krishna for कृष्ण and Rigveda for ऋग्वेद. This pronunciation is also common among contemporary Sanskrit scholars. An r-colored vowel is produced when the tip or blade of the tongue is either curled upward (retroflex articulation) or when the tongue's tip is lowered while the back of the tongue is bunched. Both articulations result in a similar auditory effect: a lowering of the third formant frequency. Although rare, r-colored vowels are found in some non-standard varieties of Dutch and in rhotic accents of English, such as General American. In English, these vowels are often analyzed phonemically as underlying [ɚ] or [ɝ] rather than as syllabic consonants. Depending on their position in a word (initial, medial, or final), it has been suggested that there are at least 21 distinct allophones of [ɚ] in English. In General American English, r-colored vowels are typically written using vowel-r digraphs. Any vowel can be used in this context. For example, the word iron contains an r-colored vowel, represented phonetically as [aɪɚ]. In singing, many English-speaking vocalists who normally use r-colored vowels in speech replace them with their non-rhotic equivalents when singing in English. However, this is not universal, as many Irish singers retain r-colored vowels in their singing. In English, the pronunciation of vocalic /r/ is highly variable due to inconsistencies in vowel combinations. These inconsistencies can lead to articulation or speech disorders, particularly in young children learning to produce /r/. The sound /r/ is challenging to master and is one of the most frequently misarticulated sounds for several reasons: It can function as either a consonant or a vowel. There is no single, defined manner or place of articulation for /r/. It is a later-developing sound in speech acquisition. Its correct pronunciation is not dependent on spelling. Evaluation and treatment of vocalic /r/ issues are typically conducted by speech-language pathologists. In Mandarin Chinese, the rhotacized ending of certain words is a key feature distinguishing speakers of the Beijing dialect from speakers of other Mandarin varieties. This phenomenon is called Erhua by Mandarin speakers. In many cases, the -r suffix is added to indicate changes in meaning. In simplified written Chinese, this change is represented by the suffix 儿. If the word ends in a nasal, the final consonant is lost, and the vowel becomes nasalized. In the 1930s, the Dravidian language Badaga exhibited two degrees of rhoticity across all five of its vowels. However, few speakers maintain this distinction today, and it is now limited to one or two vowels. An example includes non-rhotic [a], slightly rhotacized [a˞], and fully rhotacized [a˞˞].
